content.title: About
content.content: Turnip is a root vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, cultivated in temperate regions. Raw turnip has a crisp texture, a mildly peppery and refreshing flavor, and a pale white or pinkish flesh. It is commonly used in salads, as a crunchy snack, or as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip belongs to the same family as cabbage, broccoli, and mustard.
There are over 200 turnip varieties, differing in color, shape, and pungency.
Historically, turnips were used in folk medicine to aid digestion.
Turnips grow quickly – from sowing to harvest usually takes 3–4 weeks.
The edible part is the swollen stem base, not a true root like carrots.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Turnip provides a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: With very few calories per serving, turnip is an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in turnip aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in turnip have antioxidant properties that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turnip, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Consuming large amounts of turnip can cause bloating due to its raffinose content.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High vitamin C levels may enhance the effect of certain drugs, for example anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw turnip is usually washed, trimmed, and eaten whole, sliced into rounds, or cut into matchsticks. It can be added to salads, sandwiches, snack plates, or used as a garnish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store turnip in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp cloth to keep it crisp for up to 2 weeks. Rinse thoroughly before consumption.
